events.title: Hasan Piker on "The Axios Show": America worse than al-Qaeda "pound for pound"
events.summary: LOS ANGELES — Left-wing streamer Hasan Piker tells Axios he believes America conducts more terrorism in the world than al-Qaeda, the terror network that carried out the 9/11 attacks. "Pound for pound as far as the number of deaths, yes," Piker said in an exclusive interview for a new episode of "The Axios Show." Piker added: "We have caused tremendous terror all around the world." Why it matters: Piker is one of the most popular streamers on Twitch, and his history of incendiary statements has become central to Republicans' attacks in the critical Senate race in Michigan since Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed had Piker campaign for him in the primary. Driving the news: Piker's comments to Axios came in response to a question about his previous statement that "America is the top dog in terrorism." Piker pointed to the deaths of more than 100 people at an elementary school in Minab, Iran, earlier this year. The AP found evidence that at least one U.S. missile struck the school. "If you're killing 140 schoolgirls, that is an act of terror," he said. "This doesn't mean that all Americans are terrorists, but the reality of the matter is we have to create an environment of accountability to ensure things like that never happen again." The Trump administration has not yet released findings from a Pentagon investigation, and an exact death toll is not known. The big picture: Republican-affiliated groups already have spent nearly $3 million in ads attacking El-Sayed over his affiliation with Piker, according to the tracking firm AdImpact. Most of the ads feature a clip of Piker in 2019 saying that "America deserved 9/11." He apologized for the remark and has since argued that the terror attacks were part of "blowback" from U.S. involvement in the Middle East in previous decades. "This doesn't justify the action, mind you," he told Axios. "This is more so analysis to stop further violence from taking place, both violence in the region, but also violence in the home front as well." Michigan's GOP Senate nominee, Mike Rogers, also frequently ties Piker to El-Sayed. In his speech at the recent Republican midterm convention in Dallas, Rogers said: "Abdul El-Sayed has chosen Hasan as his running mate. Together, they attack America, excuse extremism, and treat our country like the villain." El-Sayed has largely dodged questions about Piker and occasionally appeared irritated by them, often referring to him as just a "streamer in California." "The reason I talk to Hasan isn't because of Hasan, it's because of the 3 million people who pay attention to what he has to say," El-Sayed told Fox 2 Detroit Tuesday night at a debate where Rogers didn't show up. "Too often the way that our politics happen is that we're told who we cannot talk to," El-Sayed added. In a statement to Axios on Wednesday, El-Sayed said, "I do not agree with this statement [on al-Qaeda], nor do I give much weight to the statements made by a social media streamer. I am more concerned with the dangerous policies of Donald Trump and Mike Rogers that are raising the prices of gas, groceries and healthcare for Michiganders."

events.title: AI's imminent hacking threat is hiding in plain sight
events.summary: An unprecedented wave of AI-powered, human-driven cyberattacks is coming, security experts say — and it's a far more urgent risk than theoretical scenarios in which AI wipes out humanity. Why it matters: The great September AI panic — which spread from boardrooms to Congress to American households in the last week — may have missed the point. Powerful models with advanced cybersecurity capabilities are already allowing attackers to bypass the human bottleneck that has long prevented most hacking campaigns from reaching industrial scale. Executives and former officials have told Axios they fear automated cyberattacks that turn off critical services like the power grid, or attackers using AI agents (like the ones that breached Hugging Face) to hack self-driving cars or create a botnet that takes over the whole internet. Driving the news: OpenAI on Wednesday disclosed six new incidents in which its models concealed mistakes, sought unauthorized credentials, uploaded files to the public internet or communicated across supposedly isolated training environments. The big picture: Rather than seeing recent safety failures at OpenAI and other frontier labs as terrifying instances of agents running amok , seasoned cybersecurity experts instead say they represent cautionary tales illustrating what will happen when powerful models meet poor security controls. "The more we have been peeking under the hood to understand exactly what happened, the more we realize that there was a lot of human error in the picture," Michele Catasta, president and head of AI at app builder Replit, told Axios. For the record: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has said the Hugging Face breach was the "first security incident that I have felt very viscerally," and the company has implemented new internal controls. Kai Chen, alignment research lead at OpenAI, told Axios in an interview Wednesday that the safety incidents they've faced are due to both internal systems and advancing model capabilities. "It's true that model capabilities have grown faster than we expected, but there are also things internally that we can change and improve," Chen said. "We need to step up to meet this new era of AI development, and voluntary disclosures should be a part of that." Between the lines: Catasta and others who spoke at an Imagination in Action event at Google's headquarters Monday offered a view that the imminent threat from cyber intrusions is formidable. "I don't worry about the machine waking up and deciding to end us," Bugcrowd CEO Dave Gerry told Axios. "What I worry about is a system with too much access doing exactly what it was told without the necessary adversarial testing." Mimecast CEO Ranjan Singh told Axios that the real risk is happening today with AI agents that have access to sensitive documents and internal corporate systems. "It is right to sound the alarm, but the risk doesn't require an internet-scale swarm to become real," he said. "Most organizations can't tell you who or what that agent is, what it's allowed to touch, or who's accountable when it does something it shouldn't." What to watch: A number of business executives are saying behind closed doors that they plan to hold frontier labs accountable for the behavior of their models. If they get hacked as Hugging Face did, expect litigation. A senior executive at a top hedge fund who spoke to Axios said his first call, if his firm had suffered a similar attack, would be to his general counsel to prepare a lawsuit. events.title: Flock Once Touted Its Cameras as ‘Made in the USA.’ Now It’s Not So Clear
events.summary: Flock CEO Garrett Langley has said the company made its first license plate cameras in his Atlanta home, permanently scratching his dining table with drill marks. A decade later, where the company assembles its signature—and fiercely debated —product has become more of a mystery. For years, Flock touted publicly that its devices were produced in the United States. But more recent marketing materials from the company reviewed by WIRED no longer specify where its cameras come from. One US manufacturer that previously identified Flock as a customer quietly removed a mention of the company from its website earlier this year as public backlash against the company’s surveillance technology grew. The startup has become the subject of a nationwide protest movement that has prompted dozens of local governments to abruptly stop using its cameras. Congress is also considering legislation that would cut federal funding to states that fail to limit use of Flock and other license plate readers. While police have argued the cameras are crucial tools for deterring and solving crime, activists have criticized Flock for enabling officers to track the cars of their exes , share footage with immigration authorities , and follow the movements of pedestrians . But Flock’s manufacturing supply chain has received scant attention, even though where its hardware is produced could have implications for US national security. WIRED spoke with current and former Flock employees and supply chain analysts, reviewed data from US import records, and watched past marketing videos featuring Langley to piece together the first account of how its hardware pipeline has evolved. Flock’s cameras largely rely on suppliers around the world that provide non-custom parts, which are also used in products from other companies. “Our value is in the aggregation and the packaging of all of these things … in a nice waterproof, consumer-friendly device,” Langley said in one marketing video from 2021. Import records collected by ImportGenius show the company has been increasingly bringing “commodity” cameras, radar systems, and other components over from Primax Electronics in Thailand. Primax is based in Taiwan, but has manufacturing facilities in China, Thailand, and elsewhere. “My understanding is that these are components, but it looks like Primax manufactures whole security camera solutions,” ImportGenius’ analyst Lynn Hughes says. “Quite a few shipments include ‘Radar’ in the product description which might be related to the radar sensor pods they’re attaching to their cameras.” Flock didn’t respond to most of the detailed questions WIRED asked for this story, though it did provide some general information. “All products that Flock builds are National Defense Authorization Act compliant,” Flock spokesperson Paris Lewbel said in an email, referring to a US law that effectively bars government contractors from using parts made by a handful of Chinese tech companies over security concerns. Cris van Pelt, creator of the anti-Flock advocacy project Have I Been Flocked, says that while where the cameras are made may have relatively minor implications for US communities, the lack of transparency about their origins underscores a broader problem . “It all speaks to the fact that there is no real oversight, and that tens of thousands of literal and figurative black boxes are being installed on American roads,” van Pelt says. “If any part of the supply chain is compromised, we would never know. That’s a much bigger problem than where the final product is assembled.” The earliest Flock prototypes were made using cameras ripped out of Android phones bought on Alibaba, which were then attached to batteries and soldered onto a solar panel, Langley recalled in one video. The goal was to prove that a useful device could be created from parts collectively costing between $200–300. (WIRED reported earlier this week that Flock’s cameras continue to use smartphone-style processors and leave significant data unencrypted.) As Flock began securing contracts with homeowners associations, it shifted into a corporate office that also doubled as an assembly line. Langley described the setup as fun, but also unprofessional and arduous—pallets of parts shipped in from China had to be dragged a quarter of a mile through the building multiple times a week. Around 2020, Flock moved its assembly line to a WeWork-style warehouse facility in Atlanta, according to a marketing video produced by the space’s operator. A handful of Flock employees cranked out as many cameras as they could, with engineers assembling the main camera device and less technical staff attaching solar panels and mounts. Rather than opening up warehouses, Flock stored cameras in self-storage locations across the country for its installation crews to retrieve as needed, according to two former employees.

events.title: Oregon Lawmakers Seek to Open Up Affordable Housing Records Following ProPublica’s Reporting
events.summary: Illustration by Jovelle Tamayo/ProPublica. Source images: Records obtained by ProPublica, iStock. Two Oregon lawmakers want to end an unusual exemption in the state’s records law that has kept the public from learning how hundreds of millions of dollars in taxpayer money is spent on subsidized housing — and the effort has already landed key industry support. Rep. Pam Marsh, chair of Oregon’s House Committee on Housing and Homelessness, told ProPublica that she plans to introduce legislation next year to eliminate a law that shields key details of state spending on low-income housing . The southern Oregon Democrat said she didn’t realize the documents were being kept secret until reading about it in a ProPublica story. She said previous leaders of her committee told her they were also unaware. “I think this is an issue that will have very broad interest,” Marsh said. State Sen. Khanh Pham, a Portland Democrat and chair of the Senate Committee on Housing and Development, said she also wants the Legislature to tackle the issue in its next session. Meanwhile, a lobbying group for low-income housing developers, lenders and related businesses, Housing Oregon, said it strongly supports repealing the secrecy provision; the organization has asked the state to disclose more about projects that it funds in the meantime. “Oregon’s affordable housing providers share the public’s interest in ensuring that public investments in housing are used effectively, responsibly, and with visibility,” said Kevin Cronin, a spokesperson for the group. “The questions raised in your recent ProPublica article regarding development costs deserve serious attention.” Cronin said Oregon can increase transparency around development costs “while still protecting genuinely proprietary or competitively sensitive information.” “More consistent reporting of costs and outcomes will help policymakers, providers, researchers, and the public understand where the system is working and where it needs improvement,” Cronin said. ProPublica highlighted Oregon’s secrecy around low-income housing in August. Since 2021, our story noted, Oregon has given developers an unprecedented $1.4 billion, and the cost of developing each low-income apartment has nearly doubled, to $540,000. Dozens of projects are lined up for another $850 million in future state funding, and costs are expected to continue rising. Read More Oregon Is Spending More Than Ever on Low-Income Housing. A State Law Keeps the Details Secret. “We are spending, as you said, a lot of money on the development of affordable housing,” Marsh said. “We really need to understand what it is that we’re funding, how much it costs, why it costs that much, and be able to justify the investments that we’re making.” In other states, researchers and journalists have used the financial records from subsidized housing projects to investigate their spiraling costs and the drivers behind the growing price tag. Marsh said after reading the ProPublica story that she “pretty much immediately” looked up the provision in Oregon public records law that officials cite for keeping cost details secret. She said financial documents that show where a project’s money is coming from and what it’s going to should be public and easily accessed. She said she would like to see them posted online as part of the public materials that Oregon’s Housing Stability Council receives for each project before awarding subsidies. Pham, in a written statement, said: “It’s imperative that Oregonians can trust that our state government is investing in affordable housing as cost-effectively as possible. I appreciated ProPublica’s reporting on Oregon’s inadequate public records law that hinders our ability to monitor how affordable housing funds are being spent, and I’m hopeful legislators can address this next year.” Oregon’s Sunshine Committee, which reviews public records exemptions and recommends ones that could be rolled back, is also examining the exemption for housing financials as a result of ProPublica’s coverage, co-chair Charlie Fisher said. It’s not clear where opposition to repeal efforts, if any, might arise. Officials in Washington and California, where the details of state spending on subsidized housing are available to the public, have said it hasn’t interfered with low-income housing efforts. Oregon Housing and Community Services, the state housing agency that persuaded lawmakers to create the records exemption in 1997, cited the law in redacting major sections of developers’ cost reports that ProPublica requested in May. The agency’s current executive director, Andrea Bell, told ProPublica in July that she is committed to transparency but that the agency is following the law as it stands today.  Asked to comment this week about whether the agency would support efforts to change the law, a spokesperson said by email that state agencies don’t take positions on bills. “OHCS appreciates the opportunity to review the legislation” that’s introduced in 2027, the spokesperson wrote. The post Oregon Lawmakers Seek to Open Up Affordable Housing Records Following ProPublica’s Reporting appeared first on ProPublica .

events.title: Flydubai expects higher fuel costs, travel curbs and aircraft delays to limit growth
events.summary: Soaring jet fuel prices, international travel advisories and aircraft delivery delays are frustrating flydubai 's growth plans, with higher fuel costs being passed on to customers. The airline has hedged a “big part” of its position against higher jet fuel prices. Still, the rising costs are reflected in its air fares, chief executive Ghaith Al Ghaith said at Arabian Travel Market in Dubai on Wednesday. Jet fuel is the “biggest headache” because sudden price swings make it hard to cash in on higher air fares due to the fuel market's unpredictability, he added. “Your fare has to reflect your cost,” Mr Al Ghaith said. “Whenever the costs increase – in this case, the fuel – our fares are reflecting the fuel price.” The majority of flydubai's aircraft deliveries have also been postponed to the end of the year, with its Boeing 787s coming in 2028 after repeated delays in 2026 and 2027, leading to added costs in terms of crew training and route openings. The jet delays have not offered operational relief during the travel disruptions from the Iran war, he said. “We are totally not seeing any benefits from aircraft delays because we want to be at full capacity to start business when it comes back with a vengeance,” Mr Al Ghaith said. The travel advisories imposed by some western governments on several Middle East countries during the regional conflict are having a “big negative” impact on inbound travel, particularly from Europe, he said. “We believe that as soon as all of these restrictions are lifted, the traffic will come back,” Mr Al Ghaith said. Growth outlook The airline boss is optimistic about the airline's recovery from the seven-month conflict, betting that demand will return quickly once restrictions ease. Flydubai is already operating at 85 per cent of its capacity and expects to return to prewar levels, or exceed them, by the end of 2026 as it takes delivery of 11 aircraft. “We really had a very good summer; it encourages us that a full recovery is around the corner,” he said. The airline now flies to 130 destinations out of its prewar network of 140. Markets such as Eastern Europe are recovering faster than others, with forward bookings “almost back to normal”. “Our biggest disadvantage currently, especially in Europe, is all of these advisories that are still ongoing,” he said. Mr Ghaith said the airline was not behind its prewar growth target. “We are taking all the aircraft that we are supposed to take; we are manning up for this operation because you have to be ready for the day after when the business will come, and it will come with a vengeance.” The airline still expects to make a profit despite the higher costs and travel disruptions, with no redundancies and continued hiring. “We always work on a target that we will make money. This is always in our DNA,” he said. “Our cash flow is as strong as it was before the war.” Mr Ghaith declined to quantify the cost of seven-month war disruptions, saying it is “significant but it is manageable”. “If we end up making money, even a little money, and sustaining our size, that is a target, because then when the business comes back, you will be bigger to absorb most of it,” he said. In 2027, flydubai plans to take delivery of up to 17 aircraft. “We are very confident that it will be a great year for us,” Mr Al Ghaith said. Looking ahead, the airline continues to invest in its long-term growth with an order book of 300 planes, a focus on expanding its premium products and a recent foray into cargo. Its upcoming Boeing 787s and Airbus A321 jet deliveries will open new destinations, with China a “big part” of its future plans, Mr Al Ghaith said.

events.title: Trump’s Saudi ambassador pick faces early hurdles
events.summary: The News President Donald Trump’s pick for ambassador to Saudi Arabia, Rep. Wesley Hunt, R-Texas, is staring down a potentially difficult confirmation fight due to hurdles from a tight Senate calendar and skepticism among Republicans. Hunt’s nomination this week came just months after he finished third in the Texas Republican Senate primary. Hunt had entered the race against Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, and Attorney General Ken Paxton, turning the contentious contest into a three-way fight. Now Trump has tapped Hunt, a former Army officer who served twice in Saudi Arabia as a diplomatic liaison, for the high-profile diplomatic post. Retiring Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., could be an obstacle to Hunt’s confirmation and is likely to block Hunt’s nomination from moving as part of any large, en bloc nomination package. Tillis has previously used nominations as leverage to press the Trump administration on other issues; he’s currently holding up Kari Lake’s nomination to be ambassador to Jamaica, for instance. Asked about Hunt’s nomination, Tillis told Semafor, “I gotta look into the details.” “Right now, with the limited number of session days that we have left, if they don’t get into an en bloc package, they’re going to die,” Tillis continued. “That’s how I’m holding Kari Lake. I mean, there’s some people saying, ‘Please let her go to Jamaica,’ but the reality is once she gets Senate confirmed, she could go other places in acting roles. And that’s what I’m not going to allow.” “The truth is, the odds that I’ll let him go as an en bloc nominee are almost zero, but it needs some more work,” he said. The timing could also give Tillis additional leverage. The Senate is in its final legislative sprint through October before adjourning ahead of the midterm elections, meaning it would be difficult to fit a confirmation hearing, committee vote, and potential floor vote into the remaining calendar. If Hunt’s hearings slip until after the midterms, the calculus could change entirely — particularly if the Republicans lose seats in the Senate. Unified Republican support could also be a challenge. Asked about Trump’s pick, Cornyn told Semafor he is an “interesting choice. An interesting choice in many, many ways.” He declined to weigh in further. When Hunt ran against Cornyn and Paxton in the Texas Republican Senate race, the contest grew increasingly bitter as the primary unfolded. Cornyn’s campaign called Hunt “ fake MAGA ,” and Hunt responded by saying Cornyn’s record “ reads like a registered Democrat .” Cornyn’s reaction — after the two Republicans spent months attacking each other on the campaign trail — adds further uncertainty as Hunt seeks Republican support. Other members of the Foreign Relations Committee were cautious. Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., told Semafor, “I don’t know him well enough, so looking forward to seeing more.” Sen. Lisa Murkowski, R-Alaska, told Semafor, “You’re that first person that’s mentioned that name.” To be sure, Hunt has some early support: fellow Texan Sen. Ted Cruz told Semafor, “I think Wesley’s terrific.” Know More Hunt also has a potential vulnerability in his own record, particularly given the country he has been nominated to serve. In December 2025, Hunt posted a video describing his time as a diplomatic liaison officer in Saudi Arabia after the US operation that killed Osama bin Laden. Hunt said he stopped going to work for two weeks because he feared bin Laden sympathizers in Riyadh could target American forces. “These are our allies that we are working with every single day, and we were actually fearful of our lives,” Hunt said at the time. “Now, imagine letting people, with that mindset, come to our country, and you wonder why we are waking up to having dead national guardsmen… the mentality of these people never ended. It never stops. The jihad never ends. We are the infidel.” The comments could become a focus of questioning when Hunt appears before the Foreign Relations Committee. Hunt’s office did not respond to a request for comment. In a post on X after the nomination was announced, Hunt said he was “profoundly grateful to President Trump for his confidence in me and for the extraordinary honor of being selected.” Step Back Trump nominated Hunt at a time Saudi Arabia faces increased military pressure from Iran-backed forces. Houthi fighters in Yemen have increased attacks against targets in Saudi Arabia, and the kingdom’s East-West oil pipeline, a key route for Saudi crude exports, has shut down amid attacks. With Saudi Arabia facing intensified security challenges and seeking increased US support, Hunt’s nomination could be a welcome signal to Riyadh by telegraphing the importance of the relationship. There is also a broader shortage of confirmed US ambassadors in the Middle East. For Saudi Arabia, having a confirmed ambassador in Riyadh would provide another direct channel to the Trump administration, and in the case of Hunt, one with an extensive military background and close ties to congressional Republicans.

events.title: Senators sought to add AI antitrust exemption to defense bill
events.summary: The Scoop Senators had secured a narrow antitrust exemption for AI companies in annual must-pass defense policy legislation earlier this year before negotiations over the measure were delayed, according to people familiar with the matter. Senators included the national security-focused antitrust exemption as part of a larger so-called manager’s package of amendments to the bill, which the leaders of the Senate Armed Services Committee file each year. Specifically, the package would have included a proposal from Sens. Jim Banks , R-Ind., and Adam Schiff, D-Calif., granting AI companies a limited antitrust exemption for sharing intelligence with one another and coordinating defenses against Chinese spying and distilling of AI models, and addressing other risks to advanced systems such as cybersecurity incidents. The package had approval from Armed Services Committee leaders, Sens. Roger Wicker, R-Miss., and Jack Reed, D-R.I., the people said. Senate Democrats blocked debate on the annual bill over the summer in objection to President Donald Trump’s handling of the Iran war. It would have to survive negotiations with the House. The effort, which hasn’t been previously reported, takes on new relevance as AI companies, led by Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, advocate for a different type of antitrust exemption that allows them to coordinate on pacing the development of their technologies. That idea, fueled by concerns about risks posed by the fast-advancing technology, has drawn criticism from members of the Trump administration, as well as members of Congress from both parties. “You have a basic obligation to make your products safe. Do not demand antitrust waivers or liability waivers in exchange for that,” Trump’s former AI adviser, David Sacks, said in an interview with Bloomberg earlier this week. Know More While Amodei has suggested an antitrust waiver for coordinating on capability slowdown, the proposal from Banks and Schiff is decidedly narrower. It focuses on Chinese espionage and distillation, or the practice of an AI model training on a more sophisticated model to steal techniques. An earlier announcement of the proposal said it would allow for “coordinating responses to risks involving loss of operational control over advanced AI systems” — which the people said relates to incidents like the Hugging Face attack by OpenAI agents — and letting researchers share information with one another. Lawmakers enacted a similar policy for companies through the 2015 Cybersecurity Information Sharing Act , which protects companies from antitrust liability when they share cyber threats with government agencies or one another. It’s unclear whether the current debate over AI safety — or potential White House opposition — will change the fate of the provision. If it passes the Senate, the defense bill will need to be reconciled with the House’s own version before it can reach Trump’s desk. Not everyone in the AI industry is lobbying for the broader carveout as pushed by Amodei: OpenAI’s chief global affairs officer, Chris Lehane, recently said such an exemption for labs to be able to coordinate on pacing was unnecessary. John Connell, Google’s vice president of government affairs and public policy, said in July that the bill from Banks and Schiff would “give the AI industry clear rules of the road to share threat intelligence and collaborate on much-needed standards and benchmarks.”

events.title: Judge orders Microsoft to spill internal docs and scour execs' comms in secondhand licensing case
events.summary: The legal spat between secondhand software reseller ValueLicensing and Microsoft took another turn this week: a consent order was published with demands for documents from past and present Microsoft head honchos, and a planned case management conference was canceled. Several requests in the order revolved around a historic, potentially explosive internal document written by Microsoft entitled the "Second-Hand Software" (SHS) Presentation. ValueLicensing and Microsoft agreed to vacate the case management conference ahead of its scheduled date on September 14, 2026. The result is the Consent Order [PDF], which, unsurprisingly, focuses on locating and asking for the disclosure of Microsoft documents that may bear on the reseller's allegation that the company offered incentives for customers to shift to subscription services in return for not selling their pre-owned licenses. The confidentiality designation applied to several documents in the case has also been lifted. In addition, there are many references to a June 2013 document that Microsoft disclosed on December 22, 2025, entitled "Second-Hand Software Presentation" (SHS Presentation). June 2013 was a busy time for Microsoft: it had launched the Office 365 subscription service two years previously, but there was a question over what to do about those customers with perpetual licenses that Microsoft wanted to move into the brave new world of "an always-up-to-date cloud service, at a predictable monthly subscription." While the content of the SHS Presentation has yet to be made public, the Consent Order treats it as a "Known Adverse Document," meaning it is unlikely to be good news for Microsoft. Furthermore, the consent order requires Microsoft to explain by October 31 why it had not disclosed it earlier. This case was filed in 2021 and yet it took until the end of 2025 for Microsoft to produce the presentation. Microsoft was also asked to conduct extensive, unredacted disclosure searches across its corporate mailboxes and SharePoint accounts of high-level executives for search terms including "antitrust," "used licenses," "second hand", and "Value Licensing," between July 3, 2012 and June 1, 2020. It has until November 30 to produce any documents found during the search. Execs whose mailboxes and document repositories must be searched include Richard Chin, currently a Corporate VP at Microsoft responsible for the company's monetization approach and who was a General Manager between 2012 and 2020 working on pricing, licensing, and the business models in the Cloud and AI world. Kevin Turner, who was Chief Operating Officer at Microsoft from 2005 to 2016, is also on the list. As for confidentiality, the consent order stated, "No blanket or default designation of such documents as 'Restricted' or 'Confidential' shall be applied." Instead, it'll be on a document-by-document basis and "limited to the precise words, figures or passages said to be sensitive; and be supported by specific reasons rather than general assertions." "Defendants shall disclose by no later than 4pm on 30 November 2026 any further documents they have identified relating to the same or similar matters addressed in the SHS Presentation." Microsoft will also keep ValueLicensing apprised of its progress every 21 days. Microsoft told The Register it had no comment to make on the Consent Order. ValueLicensing boss Jonathan Horley said, "ValueLicensing have been working to get appropriate disclosure for some years and this Order is the result of that work and more recently disclosed documents. "This is a further stage enabling a better understanding of how Microsoft dealt with the second-hand software market which brings a liability trial one stage closer." The case has had several twists over the years, not least Microsoft's "Hail Mary" attempt to make it about copyright rather than the allegation that it deliberately stifled the sale of secondhand software licenses. This latest turn might eventually give an intriguing insight into how the US biz dealt with the market while encouraging customers to embrace subscriptions. Time to break out the popcorn, perhaps? ®

events.title: Why Package Digital Twins Are So Hard To Build
events.summary: Key Takeaways: Package twins must track what manufacturing actually builds, not just design intent. Missing process and supplier data can undermine otherwise precise simulations. Coupled physics and ongoing calibration keep models tied to physical reality. A chiplet can be fully characterized, tested, and considered known good, but none of that guarantees it will stay that way after it’s placed into a different package. While the chiplet itself may be unchanged, nearly everything around it can move. A different substrate can alter the mechanical and electrical environment, a different thermal interface can change how heat leaves the device, and a new power envelope can increase how much heat needs to leave in the first place. A thermal path that worked in the first product can cause throttling in the second because the surrounding package and cooling assumptions have changed. By the time the chiplet is assembled into another package, engineers may be dealing with a different system altogether, which is why package models can’t stop at the die boundary, and why the added complexity makes package digital twins so difficult to achieve. That is the basic problem facing digital twins for advanced packaging. They have to predict how known components will behave after integration and eventually inside a larger system. “A chiplet may be characterized and validated in one package or product SKU, then reused in a different package stack, substrate, cooling approach, or power envelope,” said Kenneth Larsen, senior director of product management at Synopsys . “The chiplet has not changed, but its electrical, thermal, and mechanical environment has.” Fab vs. packaging: A different kind of twin Digital twins are starting to be used in semiconductor manufacturing, but the comparison with front-end fabs needs some clarification. A fab process twin can be enormously complicated, incorporating equipment behavior, process history, and statistical learning. The difference is that much of that complexity remains inside a relatively well-defined manufacturing environment. “A fab process twin is extremely complex, so I would not frame this as fab being easy and package being hard,” Larsen said. “The difference is the nature of the problem. A fab twin is usually deep within one manufacturing environment, one process technology, and one managed flow of equipment, materials, process data, and statistical learning. A package digital twin has to solve a broader integration problem — how a multi-die system is realized across silicon, substrate, assembly, manufacturing variation, test, and reliability learning.” That broader integration problem changes what the twin has to represent. In heterogeneous integration, the package is increasingly part of the system architecture, so electrical, thermal and mechanical behavior cannot be optimized independently. Engineers already have effective tools for each of those domains, but they don’t become a package twin simply by running next to one another. The harder problem is keeping them synchronized around the same physical package as it moves from design to manufacturing. Manufacturing results also need to feed back into those models as the package is revised. “The package, silicon, substrate, materials, thermal solution, and manufacturing assumptions have to be explored together,” Larsen said. “If they are optimized separately, the digital twin becomes a late-stage validation artifact. That is not where the value is.” The boundary also becomes less obvious once the package moves onto a board and into its eventual system. Conditions outside the package can change its behavior, which means some of that context has to travel with the model. “An end-to-end package digital twin requires visibility across the entire lifecycle, from wafer fabrication through assembly, test, and ultimately system operation,” said Joon Ahn, vice president of global factory IT and automation at Amkor . “Some key process information originates upstream in foundry operations or downstream in customer applications.” Preserving that context would be difficult even if all of the necessary information were sitting in one place. Often, it’s not. The data hole From the OSAT perspective, much of the information needed to describe an advanced package comes from elsewhere. Some of it comes from the foundry, some from substrate and material suppliers, and some is generated only after assembly or test. Even equipment inside the same manufacturing flow may provide different types of data depending on its age and supplier. “For OSATs, an end-to-end digital twin is not a single model, but a connected ecosystem of process, equipment, production, supply chain, and traceability data,” said Ahn. “Packaging performance is influenced by interactions among multiple process steps. Some key process information originates upstream in foundry operations or downstream in customer applications.” What an OSAT receives can be quite different from what a predictive model ideally contains. Incoming die data may include critical dimensions and wafer-sort results, but not detailed power-density or local stress maps. A substrate may arrive within nominal specifications without showing actual warpage across the production lot, while material data sheets may not capture material-specific behavior in the end device. “The downstream analysis can then look precise while missing the manufacturing reality,” Larsen said. “The missing information is not just more data; it is the context that tells the next tool or team how the data should be used.” That context can be lost even when plenty of data survives the handoff. The problem is that different parts of the supply chain may describe the same physical system in different ways. “The hardest handoffs aren’t necessarily where we have the least data. They’re usually where the data has to move between very different engineering domains,” said CP Hung, vice president of corporate R&D at ASE . “A foundry may describe die behavior one way, a substrate supplier another, and a materials company may provide properties measured under a very specific set of conditions. Then the OSAT has to bring all of that together and understand how it will behave during assembly.” That context becomes even harder to preserve when the information crosses company boundaries. The material supplier knows things about the chemistry that the equipment company doesn’t. The equipment company knows details of the process integration that may not be available to the OSAT or fab. Much of that knowledge also represents intellectual property. “We all have our own data and everybody wants to protect intellectual property,” said Sanjiv Bhatt, senior director of marketing and business development at Mitsubishi Chemical Group . “I’ve been in this industry all my life, and when we started we had a different way of collaborating. We were a lot more open as an industry, as an ecosystem.” For a package digital twin,

events.title: Negative Expansion Materials Resist Warpage
events.summary: Key Takeaways: Warpage is becoming a bigger constraint as package, interposer, and panel sizes grow. Negative thermal expansion (NTE) materials, newly on the market, can help counter warpage. Commercial NTE materials are starting to be used in semiconductor packaging, but broader adoption will depend on temperature range, compatibility of different materials, and uniform mixing and purity. Thermally induced warpage, caused by differences in the rate at which materials expand when heated, is becoming increasingly problematic in large chips and packages. The solution may be to integrate a new class of materials that actually shrink when heated. Rather than relying solely on the few substances that can shrink, companies are focusing on mixtures of materials with a lattice structure that can resist the urge to expand. Using such materials for underfill and as the packaging molding compound can add rigidity for larger packages while keeping warpage in check. Warpage as the enemy Warpage, especially in large packages and panels, occurs because of mismatches between how, for example, a substrate, a die, and surrounding molding compound behave when heated. It’s one of the biggest issues holding back the constant enlargement of package substrates, interposers, and panels. The larger the bonded area, the greater the likelihood that edge connections may be poor or fail altogether. Even before bonding, too much warpage can defeat standard manufacturing equipment features such as vacuum chucks. “The vacuum chucks will pull the warpage down, but if the warpage is too high, then you won’t get a good vacuum,” said Knowlton Olmstead, senior manager of wafer services at Amkor . Anywhere two materials meet with different coefficients of thermal expansion (CTE), warping is likely to some degree. For example, given two layers of material, if the bottom layer has a higher CTE, then it will try to expand to its natural extent. But the material above it will restrict it, assuming they’re well adhered. That will cause the edges of the bottom material to want to curl up. It’s theoretically impossible to stop all warpage if there is a CTE difference. The question becomes how much is too much. If it’s too much, what can you do about it? “We do a certain level of modeling to model the warpage beforehand, and then there’s certain levers you can pull to control the warpage,” said Olmstead. If silicon is one of the layers (as it often is), thinning the silicon can reduce the amount of warping. “You reduce the impact of the low CTE silicon if there’s thinner silicon,” said Mike Kelly, vice president, chiplets/FCBGA integration at Amkor. “In the extreme, you can make it super thin, and then it can follow the shape of whatever I’m attached to. But that ends up being a problem, because nobody wants really thin silicon for managing high power.” Warpage also impacts how new materials may be received, such as glass. “The larger the panel you’re trying to make, the more warpage you will see,” said Lang Lin, principal product manager at Synopsys . “Today we talk about micrometers of warpage, but with glass, it could be even larger — millimeters, maybe.” One approach being explored is to identify or design materials that contract when heated, giving them a negative CTE. “Negative CTE materials could be utilized in a variety of ways to offset expansion,” said Luke Prenger, research scientist IV team lead at Brewer Science . “It might depend on why the expansion needs to be offset to begin with. For things like stress management and warpage reduction, negative CTE materials can be utilized to help better match the CTEs of different materials. An example case of this would be to add filler to a polymer material, which typically has a very high CTE compared to inorganics, to reduce the overall CTE of the polymer matrix so it is closer to that of the metal layers and other components in the device. Reducing or modulating the CTE of organic layers to be closer to the inorganic layers helps in reducing warpage and overall stress build-up in a device.” Going against the grain One of the material interfaces that results in warping is the epoxy molding compound (EMC) used for fillers and underfill. It fills all the major gaps inside the package, so when the temperature changes, it can affect everything it touches. Altering the composition of that compound can mitigate the warping. The key is changing the CTE, with a negative CTE ideal for counteracting an adjacent positive one. Alternatively, mixing a positive CTE material with a negative one can alter the overall CTE of the combination. A variety of materials can exhibit true negative thermal expansion (NTE) behavior, although it often occurs within specific temperature ranges. It may also be associated with a phase change. For example, water behaves normally above 3.98 °C, below which it moves toward freezing. Ice is famously less dense than water due to its molecular structure, and so as more of the water takes on that configuration between 3.98°C and 0°C, it expands up until the final phase transition to ice. Unlike materials exhibiting true NTE behavior, other substances may consist of normal materials encased in a lattice that restricts expansion. The structure of that lattice is important in determining how anything encased in it behaves. “The key is the structure of the filler itself,” said Sanjiv Bhatt, senior director of global marketing and business development for the semiconductor business at Mitsubishi Chemical Group . Solids may have a wide range of molecular arrangements. Whereas polymers can be amorphous, inorganic materials typically have some sort of lattice structure. Materials scientists categorize the different structures and study their rheological properties (which refers to the study of how they flow). They’ll describe lattice structures, such as house-of-cards, rigid-rod, or tetrahedral. Each of these structures behave differently and can establish rigidity in one or more dimensions. What’s within the lattice (also called a matrix or a network) can also affect the flow, and the combined NTE materials reflect such a structure — a functional material within a restraining matrix. “It’s more of a network thing than a material thing,” explained Bhatt. “Not everything will form the same network. A carbon powder forms a flocculated network. If you look at a carbon fiber network, that is a reinforcing rigid-rod network. So if you are going to put a carbon fiber into a matrix, it’s like logs in a river. If I use the logs in water, it is going to have little impact on the ability of water to flow. It will restrict it some, but the water is still going to find room between them. If I put a whole bunch of clay in the water, it will muddy it up, and it will literally restrict the water movement because now you have changed the viscosity.” Caught in a cage Such a structure, a matrix encasing another material, can restrict the t

events.title: The Silicon Heartland Wants To Be America’s Next Chip Powerhouse
events.summary: Key Takeaways: Major facility investments are driving momentum for the Midwestern semiconductor industry. Workforce development remains a major structural challenge. Quantum investment in Chicago represents a major opportunity for the regional semiconductor ecosystem. The U.S. semiconductor industry has long been concentrated in established technology and manufacturing hubs, but new investments and startup activity are helping expand the industry’s footprint across the Midwest. The prospect of a thriving Midwestern semiconductor industry has long hinged on whether semiconductor companies can leverage the region’s strong base of research institutions and available workforce, logistics, and industrial infrastructure to build a regional ecosystem. Over the last several years, that trend has gained momentum, with Intel and SK hynix bringing landmark facility investments to the Midwest, major bets on the future of quantum computing being made on the shores of Lake Michigan, and significant government investment being funneled toward semiconductor growth and startup support. Defining the Midwestern ecosystem The Midwest has undergone something of a “transformation” in recent years, with signs of a real semiconductor ecosystem beginning to materialize. “There’s always been this culture of innovation, but because a lot of the semiconductor and microelectronics work had existed on the coasts, or had been elsewhere, while the Midwest was really the heart for manufacturing, there’s been this transformation to a technology-based silicon heartland ecosystem,” said Matt Casto, CEO of Midwest Microelectronics Consortium (MMEC). “New foundry capabilities are being built just north of Columbus, Ohio. Supply chain manufacturers range from water treatment capabilities to semiconductor tools. We’ve got companies in the Midwest and in the state of Ohio now that are doing material growth development. So the building blocks for semiconductor work can connect within that Midwest ecosystem through additional supply chain capabilities. Now is a generational opportunity around advanced technology, and that requires a lot more emphasis on workforce development.” The vision for this developing semiconductor ecosystem rests on a diverse technology production network that can integrate into the region’s existing manufacturing and research base. “One defining characteristic of the Midwest is its emphasis on connecting semiconductor innovation directly to manufacturing and industrial applications,” said Christopher Salomone, account management at Synopsys . “While some regions are heavily concentrated in either semiconductor design or fabrication, the Midwest is building a more integrated ecosystem that includes research institutions, advanced manufacturing, automotive technology, defense applications, and emerging semiconductor production capabilities.” One of the biggest markers of the industry’s Midwestern development has been Intel’s $28B+ “Silicon Heartland” project in suburban Central Ohio. Expected to open in the early 2030s, the facility will create 3,000 new Intel jobs in the metro Columbus area once fully operational. “Intel’s investment helped establish the Midwest as a serious contender in advanced semiconductor manufacturing and created opportunities that simply didn’t exist in this region before,” said Ted Geer, director of state government affairs for Ohio at Intel . “The Midwest has always produced exceptional engineers, researchers, and technical talent through its universities and research institutions. Too often, however, many of those graduates built their careers elsewhere. Today, students and researchers across the region can see a pathway to participate in leading-edge semiconductor manufacturing without leaving the Midwest. Organizations like MMEC are helping build on that momentum by strengthening connections between research, talent development, and the future of domestic microelectronics.” Part of the growing momentum also comes from established regional power players expanding their footprint with long-term growth in mind. “Brewer Science has been rooted in the Midwest since 1981, and our positioning isn’t incidental to the region; it’s strategic,” said Srikanth Kommu, co-CEO at Brewer Science . “We’ve demonstrated that world-class materials innovation and manufacturing can thrive outside traditional coastal hubs, which directly challenges the historical consolidation of semiconductor ecosystems. When you connect that kind of regional leadership to what we’re doing on the ground, like our acquisition of Heraeus Epurio’s semiconductor chemicals business, which brought a production facility in Dayton, Ohio, into our operations, you start to see a materials corridor forming across the Midwest that didn’t exist five years ago. Our deliberate geographic deepening through acquisitions and internal growth, from Rolla to Vichy to Springfield to now Dayton, treats our supply chain and workforce as strategic assets. This model lets us sustain margins while investing in facility upgrades, process improvements, and worker development. events.title: Beyond Scaling: The Growing Role Of Materials Innovation In Semiconductor Manufacturing
events.summary: For decades, semiconductor progress has been defined primarily by our ability to make devices smaller, faster and more powerful. But as the industry moves deeper into the AI era, scaling is becoming increasingly dependent on something less visible: the materials that make each new generation of devices possible. This shift is already apparent across many semiconductor manufacturing trends. Advanced-node scaling is creating requirements that existing materials cannot always satisfy. AI is driving extraordinary demand for compute performance while simultaneously increasing data movement and power consumption. Electrical interconnects are approaching practical limitations, while power delivery and thermal challenges are becoming system-level constraints. As a result, the future of semiconductor manufacturing will depend not simply on optimizing existing materials, but increasingly on developing and commercializing fundamentally different ones. This is not unique to semiconductors. Across industries, materials transitions have historically enabled major technological advances—from new battery chemistries to successive generations of displays. What is changing is the speed at which those transitions are occurring. Two forces in particular are accelerating materials innovation: rapidly expanding computational capabilities and a shift from conventional supplier relationships toward deeper co-development across the technology ecosystem. For semiconductor makers, the combination could fundamentally change how advanced materials move from the laboratory into high-volume manufacturing. Computational materials development Materials development has traditionally been an experimental discipline. Researchers synthesized a candidate material, characterized it, learned from the results and repeated the process. For complex materials, synthesizing a single candidate can take weeks, making extensive physical experimentation inherently slow. Increasing computational power has changed that equation. Simulation can now take place before synthesis, allowing researchers to determine which candidates warrant physical experimentation. As models, proprietary data sets and computational resources improve, researchers can screen increasingly large numbers of candidates and identify regions of material performance that existing approaches simply cannot reach. This distinction is important. The value of computational materials development is not limited to finding a better version of an existing material. It can reveal when incremental improvement is unlikely to meet the target at all. That knowledge can shorten development cycles by enabling researchers to abandon an unproductive material path earlier and redirect resources toward a fundamentally new solution. The progression from supplementary calculation to pre-experiment screening, hyper-screening and ultimately materials AI illustrates how computing is becoming embedded throughout the discovery process. For advanced semiconductor manufacturing, this capability will become increasingly valuable. Advanced node scaling materials must satisfy multiple—and sometimes conflicting—requirements involving electrical performance, thermal behavior, mechanical properties, purity, process compatibility and manufacturability. The search space is simply becoming too large for traditional trial-and-error development alone. The next step will be combining accumulated experimental knowledge with high-performance computing, materials AI and, eventually, quantum computing. The organizations best positioned to capitalize on these tools may be those with something AI itself cannot manufacture overnight: large quantities of high-quality, proprietary materials data accumulated through decades of real-world development. Collaboration is critical Computational power alone, however, cannot solve the semiconductor industry’s materials challenges. The second major change is organizational. Semiconductor development has evolved from relatively linear customer-supplier relationships toward much more integrated collaboration among device makers, equipment companies and materials suppliers. That trend reflects the growing interdependence of process, equipment and materials performance. When a new material must work within a deposition process, interact correctly with adjacent films and ultimately deliver a specific device characteristic, optimizing it independently makes less and less sense. This argues for earlier supplier engagement and more extensive semiconductor roadmap collaboration. Instead of developing a material internally and presenting it to customers late in the process, materials suppliers can work with ecosystem partners while requirements and process architectures are still evolving. Such partnerships offer another benefit that is difficult to replicate digitally: access to tacit knowledge. Formal specifications describe what a material needs to accomplish, but engineers working together often uncover process interactions, tradeoffs and practical constraints that never appear in a data sheet. Sharing that knowledge can substantially accelerate development. It may also require changing how development resources are allocated. Traditional risk-reduction models increase investment gradually as technical uncertainty declines. A partnership-driven approach does nearly the opposite: it commits greater resources earlier, creating enough differentiated material candidates to engage partners sooner and accelerate the path toward a manufacturable solution. In that sense, materials co-innovation in semiconductors is becoming as much a strategic capability as a technical one. Where the next materials transitions may occur The emerging challenges around AI illustrate why this model matters. One example is the transition from wet to dry processes for increasingly fine-pitch semiconductor structures. Continued device miniaturization can require new precursors for thin-film deposition, creating a materials challenge that combines molecular design, computational screening and process expertise. Fine-pitch precursor development is an example of this intersection between performance requirements, simulation and collaborative process development. But AI semiconductor materials requirements extend well beyond transistor fabrication. Data movement is becoming a major constraint on computing performance and energy consumption. As electrical signaling speeds increase, power requirements rise sharply, strengthening the case for optical circuits and photonic interconnects. Optical circuits are a route to significantly reducing data-center power consumption, while high-speed optical modulation is becoming critical to scaling interconnect bandwidth. These architectures create new materials opportunities—from transparent optical waveguide materials to organic electro-optic materials capable of extremely high-speed signal conversion. events.title: AI’s Storage Problem Is a Packaging Problem
events.summary: Most conversations about AI start and end with compute. But every training run and every inference query is ultimately a data problem, and data must live somewhere. Memory, and increasingly, the packaging that makes dense memory manufacturable, is doing as much to define AI system performance as the accelerators getting all the attention. AI models, cloud services, smart devices and connected systems create, process and store information at rates that would have seemed implausible a decade ago. Storage has quietly become foundational infrastructure. Consumer devices generate data continuously, from sensors to entertainment platforms. Automotive systems, particularly autonomous and connected vehicles, depend on massive volumes of stored information simply to operate safely. The result is structural, long-term demand for NAND flash rather than another consumer-driven cycle. The everyday math of a data-hungry world The growth is easy to see in ordinary digital experiences. Moving a two-hour movie from HD (1080p) to 4K increases the data required by roughly 4.7X, driven by pixel density, the added bit depth needed for HDR, and higher frame-rate targets. Photography tells a similar story: image file sizes have grown about 3X as smartphone cameras went from 12MP to 48MP, with enhanced color processing and expanded dynamic range compounding the effect. Audio has followed, a three-minute track that can grow up to 6X moving from compressed MP3 to immersive formats such as Dolby Atmos. Codec advances help. They don’t keep pace. Memory scaling must carry the rest. AI is redrawing the memory map Yole Group’s 2024 data put the stand-alone memory market at $170 billion, a 78% year-over-year rebound after two years of decline. DRAM, including HBM, accounted for roughly 57% of revenue; NAND took 40%. Heading into 2026, AI workloads are reshaping how suppliers allocate capacity. Manufacturers are expanding production of HBM and advanced DRAM nodes, prioritizing products aligned to AI performance requirements, and accelerating HBM ramps that now represent more than 10% of the total memory market. That strengthens the HBM ecosystem, but it also constrains investment in traditional DRAM and NAND capacity. NAND demand, meanwhile, keeps broadening: data center SSDs as critical storage infrastructure for AI servers; rising SSD attach rates across PCs and laptops; higher storage tiers in premium smartphones; and automotive systems where electrification and intelligent vehicle architectures require robust solid-state storage. Diversified demand supports a stable NAND outlook through 2026, even against tighter supply. From 50 packages to one The scaling story is best told in footprint. Storing 2TB in 2010, when only planar 2D NAND existed, would have taken more than 50 eMMC chips, each in a package roughly 17 x 22 mm. 3D NAND arrived in 2013 and changed the trajectory by stacking cells vertically; by 2020, 100+ layer architectures had sharply reduced the package count needed for the same capacity. Next comes wafer-to-wafer hybrid bonding, which raises interconnect density while improving electrical performance at the wafer level. It is expected to push vertical scaling well past today’s devices, toward architectures that may eventually reach 800 to 1,000 layers through multi-wafer stacking. Combined with growing QLC adoption, higher-layer 3D NAND is enabling a single eMMC device to hit 2TB. Thin, tall and reliable: the packaging problem At the package level, mobile and enterprise SSD growth is driving denser BGA packages and faster interfaces, which in turn demand tightly integrated die stacks and controller integration. Getting dies thin enough to stack higher, without giving up yield or reliability, requires coordination across the entire flow, from wafer prep through final assembly. Wafer preparation. Modern flows are engineered for 300+ layer NAND, managing die stress and warpage to prevent cracking and chipping. Key capabilities include laser grooving, ultra-fine wafer grinding, blade or stealth dicing, and automated optical inspection for crack detection. Wafers thin from roughly 700–800 µm down to as little as 25–50 µm, at which point fine grinding, polishing and backside treatments become essential to remove subsurface micro-cracks and reduce stress concentrations. Saw streets are conditioned via laser grooving or plasma pre-cut, and techniques such as dice-before-grind (DBG) and stealth dice-before-grind (SDBG) minimize edge damage. AOI runs throughout, catching cracks before compromised dies reach assembly. Die handling. As dies gets thinner, conventional handling breaks down, literally. Specialized thin-die tooling, including needle-less pickup with precisely controlled vacuum force, is required to minimize bending and prevent fracture. Wire bond architecture. At 32+ die stacks, the challenge shifts from optimizing individual steps to managing the stack as a system. Ultra-low and ultra-long loop profiles maintain clearance in tall stacks, while extended die overhang supports stair-step and zig-zag configurations. Stair-step layouts protect wire clearance; zigzag distributes stress. Customized die attach, film-on-die (FOD), film-on-wire (FOW) or spacers, prevents die sag and preserves bond integrity in controller-under-NAND configurations without adding Z-height. All of this happens inside a shrinking Z budget dictated by end applications like smartphones. Molding and warpage control. Advanced compression molding minimizes flow-induced wire sweep and distributes pressure uniformly across tall stacks. Mold cap thickness and overall material balance must be optimized against profile targets while controlling CTE mismatch. Low-stress die-attach films, carefully selected substrates and optional EMI shielding round out the materials strategy. Inspection and data analytics. Inline inspection at key stages plus unit-level traceability create the feedback loop that sustains yield — enabling early anomaly detection, rapid correlation to materials, tools or process conditions, and faster excursion containment in high-volume production. Why the OSAT role is growing Not every NAND maker is an IDM able to own the full value chain from IP and wafer fab through final assembly and test. That gap is where OSATs matter, and in today’s geopolitical environment, globally distributed manufacturing has become a strategic asset rather than a logistics footnote. Leading OSATs support consumer, industrial and automotive customers with high-stack memory packaging, unit-level traceability, wafer-level fan-out and turnkey test. Only a limited number operate true multi-region networks. As semiconductor companies prioritize diversified, geopolitically balanced supply chains, facilities spanning Asia, Europe and the United States are becoming a differentiator. events.title: Driving Power Delivery Innovations For The AI Data Center
events.summary: As AI and high-performance computing (HPC) workloads continue to scale, rising current demands are pushing traditional power delivery networks to their limits. Power delivery has become a critical challenge for modern computing systems, with current-density limitations, routing congestion and the growing complexity of multi-chip architectures creating new performance and reliability concerns. This paper explores how power delivery requirements are evolving across the accelerator, rack and data center hierarchy. It examines Intel Foundry’s power delivery innovations, including Intel 18A backside power delivery and advanced silicon capacitor technologies that improve power integrity at the die and package levels. It also highlights Intel’s advancements in integrated voltage regulator (IVR) technology, which moves power conversion closer to the point of load within the package to help address current-density scaling challenges. Rather than prescribing a single solution, the paper presents a range of approaches that architects and technologists can apply based on system requirements, performance objectives and architectural tradeoffs. What You’ll Learn Understand the key power delivery challenges shaping AI accelerators, racks and data center architectures. Explore advanced power delivery innovations, including backside power delivery, silicon capacitors and integrated voltage regulators designed to improve efficiency and reliability. Learn how to evaluate power delivery strategies and architectural tradeoffs for next-generation AI systems. Read more here . Fig.1: Backside power delivery using PowerVia. events.title: Virtual Fabrication Meets Stress Physics: Solving GAA Channel Non-Uniformity
events.summary: Gate-all-around (GAA) nanosheet transistors are revolutionizing sub-5-nm CMOS chips, but a subtle design challenge has come into focus: the mechanical stress created in the nanosheet channels does not distribute uniformly across stacked GAA transistors. Because stress reshapes the silicon band structure and directly changes carrier mobility, 1 even small imbalances between the stacked nanosheets can distort device behavior in ways that are difficult to predict from geometry alone. What causes stress non-uniformity in GAA transistors? Stress non-uniformity occurs when stacked nanosheet channels experience different strain levels during fabrication. These differences affect carrier mobility, current flow, threshold voltage, and leakage. Using SEMulator3D stress modeling, engineers can identify these variations early and optimize channel thickness, fin width, and lateral etch to improve performance. To illustrate, imagine that a GAA transistor’s stacked channels are three parallel highway lanes meant to carry traffic evenly. If one lane is smoother or wider than the others, more cars naturally shift into it. Similarly, if one nanosheet has higher stress and better carrier mobility, it could carry a disproportionate share of current, throwing off the device’s expected behavior. Fixing this stress problem requires a tool that can emulate a sequence of semiconductor fabrication steps and proactively identify stress problems in the resulting three-dimensional structure. Lam Semiverse Solutions engineers used SEMulator3D with integrated stress modeling to predict stress variations across GAA stacked nanosheets and learn how to improve stress uniformity. They identified how channel thickness, fin width, and lateral etch interact to drive non-uniform stress, revealing that a slightly thicker top channel dramatically improves uniformity. Why stress uniformity is critical for GAA nanosheet transistor performance Fig. 1: Gate-all-around field-effect transistor architecture. A GAA architecture consists of isolated silicon channels stacked vertically between the source and drain. The channels are wrapped by the gate, which controls electron transport and the on/off state of the transistor. Stress or strain in the channels reshapes the silicon band structure and the carrier mobility, saturation current, off-state current, and threshold voltage. Ideally, all GAA channels see identical stress and behave identically. In practice, process-induced variations cause them to see different stress or strain levels. The highest-stressed channel exhibits enhanced mobility and carries a disproportionate share of the current. A high-strain, low-Vt (threshold voltage) nanosheet channel can dominate off-state leakage, even if the other channels remain well controlled. This leakage current can create a spread in Vt and modify the effective turn-on characteristic of the transistor in unexpected ways. Uniform stress across the stack is therefore a critical design target, and simulation is essential because it is not obvious at the outset how to achieve it. Simulate stress in GAA nanosheet devices We created a 3D process model of the GAA device by inputting layout, process step, 2,3 and material information into SEMulator3D. We then explored predicted stress levels in the GAA channels using the generated 3D model with integrated stress analysis. Stress is generated in the channels because of lattice mismatch between silicon and the epitaxially grown source and drain regions. For the pFET, the epitaxially grown source/drain material has a slightly greater lattice constant than silicon. The nFET source/drain material has a slightly smaller lattice constant than silicon. During the replacement-metal-gate (RMG) process steps, the channels become freestanding, which allows these stressors to relax. The compressively stressed source/drain regions expand and push the pFET channels into compression, while the tensile stressed source/drain regions contract and pull the nFET channels into tension (see Figure 2). Fig. 2: Stress transfer to the silicon channel during the fabrication process. In the model, stress is solved during every major process step change: the epitaxial Si/SiGe stack, fin patterning, the gate module, source/drain growth, and the RMG module. The DOE varied the individual silicon layer thicknesses (Channel 1 to 3 thickness) and the fin width. Together, these parameters control the channel cross-section area, the primary driver of stress. We extracted the average longitudinal stress (Sigma_yy) along a vertical cut of the channels (Figure 3). Three clear peaks of stress magnitude are shown, which correspond to the three nanosheets used in our model. These stress peaks are compressive for the pFET and tensile for the nFET. The three values are visibly different, with the nFET demonstrating larger stress non-uniformity or variability. Fig. 3: Control parameters for the DoE and the Sigma_yy along the z-cut of the channels for both pFET and nFET. Figure 4 represents stress non-uniformity (referred to as “stress difference”) using a contour plot as a function of the DOE variables. The stress difference for the pFET stays under 200 MPa, while the nFET stress difference reaches 400 to 800 MPa. The stress difference is most sensitive to the topmost channel’s (Channel 3) thickness. As Channel 3’s thickness increases, the stress difference decreases. This is seen in Figure 4, as Channel 3’s thickness increases from 4 nm to 7 nm, and the red (highest stress difference) contours change to blue (lowest stress difference). This result indicates that the topmost channel (Channel 3) needs to be slightly thicker than the channels below to minimize the stress difference among channels. Fig. 4: Top channel thickness contributes most to stress non-uniformity. How fin width and lateral etch affect GAA stress uniformity The impact of fin width becomes pronounced when the fin lateral-etch ratio is high (Figure 5). The fin width is measured at the shallow trench isolation (STI) elevation for reference. The fin lateral etch ratio controls the fin taper and determines the channel width loss above the STI elevation. Fig. 5: The impact of fin lateral etch on the channel width. At a low lateral etch ratio, the fin taper is low, and channel width variation is not significant. At high lateral etch, the top channel becomes significantly narrower than the bottom.
